title: WHAT ARE YOU FEEDING YOUR MIND EVERY DAY?
paragraphs: WHAT ARE YOU FEEDING YOUR MIND EVERY DAY?
Because what enters quietly can eventually speak loudly—and some of the battles you keep calling “spiritual weakness” may begin with what you repeatedly allow to occupy your attention.
There is a frightening possibility most of us would rather not consider.
You can pray in the morning...
and spend the rest of the day feeding the very thoughts that prayer was trying to surrender to God.
You can open your Bible for ten minutes, close it, pick up your phone, and then spend hours consuming fear, outrage, lust, envy, gossip, vanity, comparison, cynicism, greed, and endless noise.
Why am I comparing myself to everybody?
Why does temptation feel stronger lately?
Why am I becoming angry so quickly?
Why does my heart feel spiritually numb?
Maybe the question is not only, “What is wrong with me?”
Maybe another question needs to be asked.
What have I been feeding my mind every day?
Because nobody eats garbage continuously and expects physical strength.
Yet spiritually, many of us attempt exactly that.
We consume whatever appears in front of us and then wonder why our inner world feels poisoned.
Another opinion designed to make us angry enough to keep watching.
And something else disappeared with it.
The ability to sit quietly before Him.
This does not mean every movie, social-media post, song, game, podcast, news report, or piece of entertainment is sinful. Scripture does not command Christians to retreat from every form of culture.
The question is not merely whether something is technically permissible.
What is it forming inside you?
Do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewing of the mind.

The Greek text places two powerful ideas against each other: συσχηματίζεσθε (syschēmatizesthe), being conformed or fashioned according to a pattern, and μεταμορφοῦσθε (metamorphousthe), being transformed. The transformation Paul describes is connected with ἀνακαίνωσις—renewal—and specifically the renewal of the νοῦς, the mind.
Jesus did not come merely to make badly behaved people slightly nicer.
The Gospel announces something far more radical.
And the Spirit of God begins transforming people who once belonged to darkness into people increasingly shaped by Jesus Christ.
Which means the battle for your mind matters enormously.
And someone reading this already knows exactly where this is going.
Because there is something you keep consuming that you would be uncomfortable watching if Jesus were visibly sitting beside you.
And before shame tells you to run away from Him, remember the Gospel.
Jesus already knew the kind of sinner He was going to the cross to save.
The cross was not God's discovery of your scandal.
The cross was God's answer to human sin.
Christ “died for our sins” and was raised again according to the apostolic Gospel proclaimed in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
So conviction is not an invitation to hide.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
You see someone's marriage and suddenly yours feels inadequate.
Someone posts a vacation and suddenly your ordinary Tuesday feels miserable.
Someone announces a promotion and your own accomplishments shrink.
Someone has the body you wish you had.
And five minutes earlier you were grateful.
Then you looked at somebody else's life.
Nothing physically changed in those five minutes.
Your children didn't become less precious.
God didn't suddenly become less faithful.
and began interpreting your life for you.
That is why guarding the inner person is not religious paranoia.
מִֽכָּל־מִ֭שְׁמָר נְצֹ֣ר לִבֶּ֑ךָ כִּֽי־מִ֝מֶּ֗נּוּ תּוֹצְא֥וֹת חַיִּֽים׃

The key command נְצֹר (netsor) means “guard” or “keep,” while לִבֶּךָ (libbekha) means “your heart.” The verse teaches that the heart must be diligently guarded because the issues or outgoings of life proceed from it.
In biblical thought, the “heart” is far richer than our modern use of the word for emotions alone. It concerns the inner person—the place of thought, desire, intention, and moral direction.
Not because everything outside you is evil.
But because everything entering you should not automatically receive permission to remain.
Your mind is not public property.
Your imagination is not a garbage dump.
And your eyes are not spiritually neutral windows through which absolutely anything should be permitted to walk.
Think about how carefully people protect things they consider valuable.
Yet sometimes we leave the gates of the mind wide open.
Stay as long as you want.
Then Sunday arrives and we ask why worship feels like trying to start a fire in pouring rain.

Jesus said something sobering in Matthew 6:22–23 about the eye and the body. His teaching belongs to the larger context of treasure, loyalty, and devotion to God—not a simplistic claim that merely seeing one bad thing automatically corrupts a person.
But the principle should still make us examine what commands our gaze.
Because whatever repeatedly captures your attention can begin discipling your desires.
Something is discipling you every day.
The question is whether it is leading you toward Christ.
Algorithms are extraordinarily good at discovering what keeps your attention.
But an algorithm does not love your soul.
It cannot reconcile you to God.
It cannot raise you from the dead.
And Jesus did not shed His blood so that the world could become your master again.
This is where the battle becomes intensely personal.
Paul tells believers in 2 Corinthians 10:5 about:
“αἰχμαλωτίζοντες πᾶν νόημα εἰς τὴν ὑπακοὴν τοῦ Χριστοῦ”

—bringing or taking every thought captive into the obedience of Christ. The Greek αἰχμαλωτίζοντες carries the imagery of taking captive, while νόημα refers to thought or that which is conceived in the mind. In context, Paul is speaking about demolishing arguments and proud obstacles raised against the knowledge of God, so this verse should not be reduced to a motivational slogan about positive thinking. Its destination is explicitly obedience to Christ.
Biblical renewal of the mind is not:
“God could never want someone like you,”
Because Christianity is not the denial of ugly thoughts.
It is refusing to crown them king.
And maybe that is precisely where somebody reading this has been losing the battle.
And beneath the blue light illuminating your face is a soul that is tired.
Not necessarily because you hate God.
You're simply exhausted from feeding two different lives.
One part of you wants Jesus.
Another part keeps returning to whatever numbs you.
You do not defeat darkness merely by staring harder at darkness.
You need something better to behold.
Paul gives Christians a beautiful filter in Philippians 4:8. He directs them toward what is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, commendable, excellent, and worthy of praise.
Think on, consider, dwell upon these things.
Christianity therefore does not merely say, “Stop thinking.”
It redirects thought toward what accords with God's truth and goodness.
There is a massive difference between an empty mind and a renewed mind.
An empty room can be filled again.
A renewed mind is increasingly occupied by truth.
So perhaps your next spiritual breakthrough does not begin with another dramatic promise.
Maybe tonight it begins with something much quieter.
Not because reading the Bible earns God's love.
Not because five chapters will purchase forgiveness.
Not because God gives salvation points for devotional streaks.
You open Scripture because the God who already speaks through His Word is more nourishing than the noise starving your soul.
“Jesus, show me what I have allowed to shape me.”
And then you become quiet enough to answer honestly.
What have you been listening to?
Whose voice has become louder than Scripture?
What fantasy have you been rehearsing?
What anger have you been feeding?
What entertainment keeps making sin look beautiful?
What voices constantly make righteousness look foolish?
What are you consuming that makes prayer harder afterward?
There is no universal Christian blacklist capable of replacing wisdom, conscience, Scripture, and obedience to Christ.
Something may not be explicitly sinful and still be spiritually unhelpful for you.
Paul's principle in 1 Corinthians 6:12 is devastatingly relevant: not everything permissible is beneficial, and he refuses to be dominated by anything.
That is a question worth carrying into your digital life.
Does it repeatedly pull you toward sin?
Does it make you more grateful or more covetous?
More sexually pure or more lustful?
More attentive to your family or more absent while sitting beside them?
or simply more like the crowd?
Legalism says your rules can make you righteous before God.
The Gospel says your righteousness and salvation are found in Christ, and the grace that saves does not leave us content to remain enslaved to sin.
Grace is not God's permission slip for self-destruction.
Maybe you have already failed today.
Maybe you deliberately clicked what you promised God you wouldn't click again.
And now the accuser is telling you there is no point returning.
But this is where our story always returns.
And yet Peter's failure was not the final chapter.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored him and called him forward.
David's story contains horrifying sin and devastating consequences, yet Psalm 51 records the cry of a man begging God for cleansing and renewal.
Paul once persecuted the church, yet the risen Christ confronted him, saved him, and transformed the direction of his life.
Scripture never tells us their scandals were secretly virtues.
But sin does not get the final word over the person who belongs to Jesus Christ.
That is why repentance is beautiful.
Repentance is not merely feeling disgusting about yourself.
You stop defending the thing destroying you.
You stop renaming bondage as freedom.
You stop negotiating with what Christ calls you to surrender.
And when you fall, you do not make peace with the ground.
Not because your repentance purchases His blood.
Maybe somebody needs to hear this tonight:
You do not need another hour of shame. You need to come back to Jesus.
End the conversation that keeps dragging you toward sin.
Put boundaries around the place where you repeatedly fall.
Ask another mature believer to walk with you.
Fill the newly opened space with Scripture, prayer, worship, service, Christian fellowship, and things that awaken gratitude for God rather than appetite for sin.
And tomorrow morning, before the world tells you what to fear, desire, hate, buy, envy, defend, or become...
Even if it is only a small passage.
Ask what it reveals about God.
Ask what it exposes in you.
Ask what Christ is calling you to believe and obey.
Carry one verse into the day.
Because eventually what you repeatedly feed begins influencing what feels normal.
And what feels normal can quietly shape what you choose.
And what you repeatedly choose can begin shaping the direction of your life.
And when you discover something inside you that does not resemble Him, don't hide it behind religious language.
Grace that can rewrite a story everyone else thought was finished.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't need to tell strangers every private detail. But you can make one small declaration that refuses secrecy.
You may discover that the battle you thought you were fighting alone is being fought by brothers and sisters all over the world.
Not as proof that you are spiritually strong, but because somebody scrolling tonight may be one click away from feeding darkness again and desperately needs to remember that Jesus is better.
Scripture does call believers to glorify God in all they do, to share what is good, and to support faithful Gospel ministry willingly rather than under compulsion.
What are you feeding your mind every day?
Because perhaps the most dangerous things entering your life are not always kicking down the door.
you invited them in with your thumb.
And perhaps tonight is the night you stop feeding what keeps starving your soul.
The scandal may explain where you have been.
Grace in Christ can change where you go next.
